1.title: Optimizing Workflows, Usage and Cost
1.text: Welcome to Module sixteen: Optimizing Workflows, Usage and Cost. This module covers optimizing workflows, usage and cost. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. What efficiency and effectiveness mean for a Claude workflow. How to save time and usage with prompts, Projects, models and settings. How to standardize and share what works. How to measure and improve over time.

1.title: Case Check-In: Cedarbrook's Monthly Report
1.text: Our running case is Cedarbrook Outfitters. Cedarbrook's Monthly Report. Finance spends two days a month building the sales report: pulling numbers, writing commentary, formatting slides. After optimization the team uses one Project, a saved method for the report format, a lighter model for the commentary draft and one review pass; the work takes half a day, and the number of corrections falls.

1.title: Efficiency and Effectiveness
1.text: Efficiency and Effectiveness. Efficiency equals the same result with less time, effort and usage. Effectiveness equals a better result: accurate, useful, on-brand, accepted by the reader. Optimize both. A fast but wrong report is not an improvement, and a perfect report that takes five days is not either. Optimize where it matters: frequent tasks, slow tasks, error-prone tasks.

1.title: Efficiency and Effectiveness, continued
1.text: Efficiency and Effectiveness, continued. The figure shows this: Levers for optimization: better prompts, Projects and Skills, model and effort choice, the right features, and a streamlined process with review.

1.title: The Main Levers
1.text: The Main Levers. Better prompts. What to do: Specific goal, audience, format; examples; batch related requests into one message. Why it helps: Fewer rounds; less usage. Reuse. What to do: Save good prompts in a prompt library; use Projects and Skills for recurring work. Why it helps: Consistency; no re-typing; shared knowledge. Project knowledge. What to do: Upload reference documents once; project content is cached and counts less when reused. Why it helps: Fewer tokens per question. Right model. What to do: Lighter model for routine and high-volume tasks; stronger for hard work (Module seven). Why it helps: Speed and usage savings. Right effort. What to do: Lower effort for routine tasks; higher only for complex ones. Why it helps: Faster; stretches usage limits.

1.title: The Main Levers, continued
1.text: The Main Levers, continued. Right feature. What to do: Chat for light tasks; web search for facts; Research only for deep work. Why it helps: Avoids expensive over-tooling. Fewer tools on. What to do: Turn off connectors and web search you do not need ("tools and connectors are token-intensive"). Why it helps: More room in the context; less usage. Short chats. What to do: Start fresh for new topics; summarize long threads (Module eight). Why it helps: Shorter context, lower usage, better focus. Lean instructions. What to do: Keep Project instructions short; put task-specific details in the chat. Why it helps: Less context overhead. Targeted edits. What to do: Edit one section instead of regenerating everything. Why it helps: Saves time and usage.

1.title: The Main Levers, continued
1.text: The Main Levers, continued. Process design. What to do: Remove unnecessary hand-offs; add review where errors matter; draft-and-review patterns (Module ten). Why it helps: Faster and safer. Usage factors: message length, attachment size, conversation length, tools (Research, web search), model choice, effort level, artifact creation and multi-step tasks such as file creation. Caches expire after inactivity, so the first message after a long break costs more.

1.title: The Main Levers, continued
1.text: The Main Levers, continued. The figure shows this: Where usage goes and how to save it: long chats, heavy tools, max effort and big attachments cost the most; restart, trim tools, lower effort and batch requests save the most. Exam tip: Efficiency answers pick the lighter, reusable, batched option (a Project, a lighter model for routine work, fewer tools, a new short chat), and keep quality checks in place.

1.title: Standardize and Share What Works
1.text: Standardize and Share What Works. Turn successful prompts into templates with blanks (audience, topic, key facts). Put the team's voice, rules and reference documents in a shared Project (Team and Enterprise allow sharing with view or edit rights). Package a repeatable method as a Skill. Write a short S O P: when to use Claude for this task, the steps, who reviews, what to check. Keep an owner and a version; review monthly. Train colleagues with real examples of good and bad outputs.

1.title: Standardize and Share What Works, continued
1.text: Standardize and Share What Works, continued. Every person writes their own prompt. Shared template and Project. Quality depends on the person. Consistent baseline. Fixes stay in one head. Lessons shared and recorded.

1.title: Measure and Improve
1.text: Measure and Improve. The figure shows this: Measure before and after: time per task, error rate, rework rounds and satisfaction show whether the change worked.

1.title: Measure and Improve, continued
1.text: Measure and Improve, continued. Time per task. How to measure: Stopwatch or ticket timestamps. Target example: Report in four hours, not sixteen. Error rate. How to measure: Share of outputs needing factual corrections. Target example: Under five percent. Rework rounds. How to measure: Average number of revisions. Target example: one or two. Usage. How to measure: Share of the session or weekly limit used. Target example: Under planned budget. Satisfaction. How to measure: Reader or colleague rating. Target example: At least four of five. Baseline: measure the current way. Change one thing. Pilot with a few users. Compare against the baseline. Keep or revert; roll out if it works. Repeat, because tools, policies and needs change.

1.title: Measure and Improve, continued
1.text: Measure and Improve, continued. Watch quality as well as speed: a quicker draft with more factual errors is not an improvement. Check in regularly on settings and knowledge so the gains do not decay (Module twelve). Exam tip: Efficiency without quality checks is not optimization: measure speed and error rate. Exam tip: Reuse beats re-typing: Projects, Skills and templates save time and usage and keep results consistent.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Goal: Efficiency (less time and usage) and effectiveness (better results). Prompts: Specific, reused, batched. Reuse: Prompt library, Projects, Skills. Model and effort: Lighter and lower for routine; stronger and higher for hard. Tools: Turn off connectors and search you do not need. Chats: Short and focused; restart with a summary. Cache: Saves usage while active; expires after inactivity. Standardize: Templates, shared Project, S O P, owner, training. Measure: Baseline, change one thing, pilot, compare, keep or revert. K P I s: Time, error rate, rework rounds, usage, satisfaction.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A team sends dozens of short, similar customer replies every day and keeps hitting its usage limit. Which change helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Routine, high-volume work suits a lighter setup and shared context.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A manager wants quicker monthly reporting. What should come first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Measuring the current time and error rate first gives a baseline, so one change at a time can be compared fairly against it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which action reduces unnecessary usage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Tools and connectors consume context and usage, so turning off the ones a task does not need reduces unnecessary consumption.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A user returns to a Project after a long break, and the first message seems to use more of the limit. Why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Caching saves usage while active; it lapses after inactivity.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Select two. Which two help standardize good results across a team? The five options are on the screen. The answers are D and E. Shared templates and a shared Project with approved knowledge spread what works, so quality does not depend on one person.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Draft time fell by half, but factual corrections doubled. What does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Speed improved but accuracy got worse, so effectiveness fell; the process needs a better check or a clearer prompt.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Which is the most efficient way to change one paragraph in a long document artifact? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Highlighting the paragraph and asking for an edit of just that part saves time and usage and leaves the rest untouched.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: D. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: C. Question five: D and E. Question six: D. Question seven: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
